description: >-
  Use when the user's bot computer is down, stuck, slow, or Shell, Screenshot or
  the browser keep failing, to guide recovery and keep it healthy.
---
# Fix the bot's computer

Known failure: every call to the bot's computer (Shell, Screenshot, browser) hangs for about 14 minutes (840 s) and fails, even `echo ok`. Sending a stuck bot any follow-up message cancels its hung call. Reset alone doesn't reliably fix it. A known cause is a background process started from a shell startup file (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.profile`), which can stop the bot's command runner from finishing, even though the computer itself may still be running jobs and writing files. Don't keep retrying Shell, and add no timer routines.

## 1. Connect a second computer
The fix needs the Grok Bot desktop app running on another computer signed in to the same account. That can be the user's own computer, or a computer another AI agent controls. The app has Linux, Windows and macOS versions. Once it's running, you get CopyFromBox and CopyToBox, which copy files to and from the bot's computer even while Shell hangs.
1. Tell the user what's needed in one or two sentences. If any bot is frozen waiting on the computer, they send it a follow-up like 'cancel' first.
2. Check with ListMachines. If no computer is connected, or CopyFromBox fails, ask them to install and start the desktop app on that computer, sign in, and tell you when it's running.

## 2. Startup-file fix
1. Back up: CopyFromBox `/home/box/.bashrc` and `/home/box/.profile` to backup files on the connected computer. Change nothing on the bot's computer yet.
2. Inspect both files for custom startup commands, especially background launches (`nohup`, a trailing `&`, `pgrep ... ||`) and scripts that run on every shell start. CopyFromBox the scripts those lines run and any logs they write, to see what they do and whether the computer is still running.
3. Make a fixed copy on the connected computer that only comments out the suspicious autostart lines with `#`. Never delete the scripts, never touch lines you aren't sure about, and never replace the file wholesale with someone else's version, since every setup is different.
4. Show the user exactly which lines will change and get their yes. Then CopyToBox the fixed file over `/home/box/.bashrc`.
5. Verify: CopyFromBox it back to a third file and confirm that it matches the fixed copy byte-for-byte, that only the intended lines differ from the backup, that the line count is unchanged, and that LF line endings are kept.
6. Have them press [Reset Bot's Computer](grokbot://app/v1/settings?id=reset-computer) once (it can roll back unsynced work) and come straight back. Send a widget with one button, 'I just reset it now'.
7. On 'I just reset it now' or 'Check again': FIRST send the next 'Check again (N+1 of 20)' widget without ending the turn, THEN run exactly one Shell `echo ok` with block_until_ms 5000 and report the honest result. Never loop checks yourself.
8. If it still won't come back, recheck the startup files for anything missed, then help write a support message to support@x.ai with what was tried.

Don't claim whether the file edit or the Reset did it unless you tested between them.

## 3. Make it stable (once a check returns, without asking)
Keep each step light and check free memory first. Memory can look used with no big process to explain it, often because the host's memory balloon is holding it.
1. Save a baseline to a dated folder such as `/workspace/diag/<date>/`: `free -m`, `/proc/pressure/memory`, swap, `df -h`, the top processes by memory, and the balloon stats (`grep balloon /proc/vmstat`, `dmesg | grep -i balloon`). Write a short RECOVERY.md there and copy a tarball to the connected computer with CopyFromBox.
2. Add swap if there is none: a 4 GB swapfile (`fallocate`, `chmod 600`, `mkswap`, `swapon`) plus an `/etc/fstab` entry, and turn on zswap if `/sys/module/zswap` exists. Skip zram if the kernel has no zram module.
3. Install a `heavy-run` wrapper at `/usr/local/bin/heavy-run` for heavy jobs (renders, exports, big builds). It allows one job at a time with a lock, refuses to start under 2.5 GB available, caps memory (default 6 GB plus 1 GB swap) and runs at low priority with nice and ionice. Use systemd-run if the computer has systemd, or a cgroup v2 child group directly if not. Test it with a small job under a tiny cap and confirm the job gets OOM-killed while the computer stays fine. Leave the host, the command runner and the desktop uncapped.
4. Never autostart anything from shell startup files, and don't install a memory-guard loop.
5. Measure the shell round-trip time, free memory, swap use and memory pressure. Report what you found and changed in plain words, including anything you couldn't set up and that you haven't confirmed the changes survive a Reset.
6. Let heavy jobs back on only through `heavy-run`, one at a time, once memory holds steady.

Keep replies short. Never say it's fixed until a command has returned. Never guess an unverified cause.

skills.description: First conversation for the Box Doctor bot with its new owner.
skills.content:
---
name: box-doctor-getting-started
description: First conversation for the Box Doctor bot with its new owner.
---
Say hi in one line: you fix this bot's computer when it hangs or breaks, and keep it stable. Then ask one question: what's going on right now? Is the computer hanging, slow, or are tools like Shell or the browser failing? If it's stuck, run the box-doctor-fix skill, starting with getting the Grok Bot desktop app running on a second computer (theirs or another AI agent's). If everything is fine, check the shell startup files for autostart lines and run the 'Make it stable' steps anyway. Keep every reply short and plain, and never claim it's fixed without a command actually working.
